sentences.text: Nanotyrannus was a mid-sized tyrannosauroid measuring approximately 17 feet in length.
Unlike the massive skulls of adult tyrannosaurs, this animal had a slender, low skull with smooth, chisel-shaped teeth that lacked serrations.
The holotype skull, which is the specimen the species is based on, measures 57.2 cm from the front tip of the premaxilla to the back tip of the quadrate.
Teeth from multiple Nanotyrannus individuals have been found embedded in the bones of herbivores.
The adult specimen known as Bloody Mary may have weighed around 704 kilograms.

The species N. lancensis was first described in 1946 by Charles W. Gilmore as a new species of Gorgosaurus, but the type specimen is actually skull CMNH 7541, collected in 1942 by David Hosbrook Dunkle.
The genus Nanotyrannus was later named by Bakker and colleagues in 1988.
Large muscle attachment sites at the rear of the skull suggest the animal could strongly flex its head side to side.

Researchers suggest that the extremely long hind limbs indicate a lifestyle adapted for pursuit predation, differing from the ambush style of tyrannosaurids, and cursorial limb proportion scores show they were more adapted for running.
A 2021 study estimated the bite force of juvenile Tyrannosaurus, including Nanotyrannus Jane, to be between 5,269 and 5,641 Newtons, which is higher than previous estimates.
A 2026 study based on bone histology found that the growth trajectories of Nanotyrannus specimens did not fit the growth curve model of adult T. rex, suggesting a distinct subadult stage.
Recent studies classify Nanotyrannus as a member of the clade Nanotyrannidae, which is the sister taxon to Tyrannosauridae.
The type species of the genus Nanotyrannus is Nanotyrannus lancensis.
Nanotyrannus morphology combines traits from basal tyrannosauroids like Moros and Xiongguanlong with those of derived tyrannosaurids.
Nanotyrannus fossils date to the Late Maastrichtian age, living during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 68 to 66 million years ago.
The animal lived in western North America in a warm, humid, and swampy environment with maritime to subtropical conditions.
Fossils of Nanotyrannid teeth, potentially belonging to Nanotyrannus, have been found in the Lance Formation.

Many researchers believe the original Nanotyrannus skull belongs to an immature Tyrannosaurus rex rather than a distinct species, though some paleontologists who previously doubted Nanotyrannus accepted it as a valid taxon after Zanno and Napoli's paper, specifically agreeing the Bloody Mary specimen is distinct from Tyrannosaurus rex.

Some scientists argue that Nanotyrannus is distinct from Tyrannosaurus because it has 15-16 teeth on each side of the upper jaw and 16-18 on each side of the lower jaw, while adult T. rex has 11-12 upper and 12-14 lower teeth, but it is debated whether the lack of serrations on Nanotyrannus teeth is a sign of juvenile development or a unique diagnostic trait of the species.
Researchers note that further testing and more data are required to determine which phylogenetic analysis of Nanotyrannus relationships is correct.
